## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nerujātaka* (Ja 379), titled in English as *Mount Neru*, is a canonical tale in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. According to its traditional introductory narrative, the Buddha related the story at Jetavana concerning a monk who took meditation subjects from the Master and resided in a frontier village [SuttaCentral]. Although the villagers initially revered him and constructed a forest hut for his residence, they repeatedly abandoned him in favor of various wandering teachers—first those advocating the permanence of matter, then annihilationists who denied immortality, and finally naked ascetics [SuttaCentral]. The story opens with the verses commencing with “Ravens and crows” [SuttaCentral].
No cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan are recorded for this text on SuttaCentral or via DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse between this work and two other Pali texts: its commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Tatiyo bhāgo*, notably sharing segments 3.4–6.4) and the *Nīti-gantha-saṅgaho Naradakkhadīpanī* (segments 3.4–5.4) [DharmaNexus]. The verses of the jātaka are also referenced in modern selections of canonical verse literature [Ānandajoti 2010].
